chapter_theme: Most of these twenty verses count acts of giving and care (water and shade, tanks and wells, alms to fasters, food to the maimed, the dying and the hungry low, care of mothers and newborns) and attach a fruit to each list, from kingship and heaven to long life and health, set among verses that strip the ascetic's outward forms, spread the sin of killing along the chain to the eater, and divide what company governs from what the mind does.

61.reading: The verse names five who live close to a man (kin who wear him down like a file and will not be checked, a wife who makes herself a wonder to others, a servant who stands unmoving like a tree, a son who turns against him, and a neighbour who watches like a hidden disease) and says that if these five are his, a life needs no other disease.
61.nuance: The predicate makes the household itself the sickness: every one of the five is someone a man cannot easily leave. Line 1 is hard (அடங்காய், பெண்வியக்க), தொண்டு is read as the servant whose simile மரம்போல் runs onto line 2, and கரம் may mean poison rather than hand, so the first three portraits are readings, not fixed.

items.claim: kin who wear one down like a file and will not be held in check are a disease
a wife who makes herself a thing for others to wonder at is a disease
a servant who stands unmoving like a tree is a disease
a son who stands against his father is a disease
a neighbour who watches one like a hidden disease is a disease

62.reading: The verse calls good the gift of water, the gift of shade, and charity within one's own house when the householder eats only after sharing, calls the founding of a temple and a hall great virtue, and says that together these bring great enjoyment.
62.nuance: The list climbs from a drink of water to a founded building, and நன்று gives way to பேரறம் at the fourth item, so the verse ranks as it counts. Only the third item carries a condition (பாத்து உண்பானேல்): charity at home counts if the giver eats after sharing. பார்அறம் is not certain in sense. The fruit named is பெரும்போகம், enjoyment, not release.

items.claim: the charity of giving water is good
giving shade is good
charity within one's own house is good, if the giver eats only after sharing
founding a temple is great virtue
founding a hall for travellers is great virtue

63.reading: The verse lists small gifts (a handful of alms, a little given afterwards, alms of gruel, salt that the giver had himself begged and brought, and a torn rag) and says that those who give them without calling them of small use gain a very great fruit hereafter.
63.nuance: The gifts are a poor man's: salt he begged for himself (எடுத்திரந்த உப்பு) and a rag. The condition is the giver's attitude (சிறுபயம் என்னார்), not the size of the gift. பின்னிறை and சிதவலிப்பு are uncertain words, so the boundaries of the second and fifth items are a reading.

items.claim: a handful of alms, given without calling it small, bears great fruit
a small measure given afterwards bears great fruit
gruel given as alms bears great fruit
salt that the giver begged and brought bears great fruit when given
a torn rag given bears great fruit

64.reading: The verse names five things that melt (butter that sees the hot fire, wax, earth that meets water, salt, and a father whose son has come to him) and says that one who gives with a heart melted like any one of them gathers fruit like a hill, however small the gift.
64.nuance: The five counted things are images, not gifts: they measure the giver's heart. Four are matter softened by heat or water; the fifth, the father at his son's approach, is the one human case and is set last, so the list ends where giving's feeling is most familiar.

items.claim: butter that sees the hot fire melts, and the giver's heart should melt like it
wax melts, and the giver's heart should melt like it
earth that meets water softens, and the giver's heart should soften like it
salt dissolves, and the giver's heart should dissolve like it
a father softens when his son comes close, and the giver's heart should soften like his

65.reading: The verse says that one who carries out five works (digging a tank, setting its bank, clearing a road, breaking ground into a ploughed field, and digging a well whose water is shared) goes sweetly to heaven.
65.domain_note: the man of means who builds for the village
65.nuance: All five are works on land and water that others use after the doer. The reward is சுவர்க்கம், heaven, not release; the Jain works keep these merits in the round of births. உளந்தொட்டு is read as breaking hard ground for the plough. The count word is fused with என்று as written (என்றிவ்ஐம் பாற்படுப்பான்).

items.claim: digging a tank leads to heaven
setting a tank's bank leads to heaven
clearing a road leads to heaven
turning ground into ploughed field leads to heaven
digging a well whose water is shared out leads to heaven

66.reading: The verse names outward forms of ascetics (wrapping the body, stripping it bare, smearing it, growing the hair long, and eating hidden and guarded) and says that if these are a virtue truly thought out one should bear what is said, but otherwise, in the Kali age, renunciation is false and household life alone is true.
66.nuance: The five forms answer to the mendicant orders of the period (clothed, naked, smeared, long-haired), though no sect is named. The close is a strong judgement for a Jain work: in கலி the household is the true path and renunciation a lie, unless the renunciant's virtue is truly considered. Line 2 (ஓர்த்து பால்மறைத்து உண்பான்மேய்) is obscure, so the fifth item is a reading.

items.claim: wrapping the body is one of the outward forms of renunciation
stripping the body bare is one of the outward forms of renunciation
smearing the body is one of the outward forms of renunciation
letting the hair grow long is one of the outward forms of renunciation
eating hidden and guarded is one of the outward forms of renunciation

67.reading: The verse says it is good to live remembering the house one was born into, holding firmly to oneself, knowing how others regard one, not living so that others say 'let him die', but so that the worthy say for many years 'may he live'.
67.nuance: The five run from the inside out: one's birth-house, oneself, others' regard, others' curse, the worthy's blessing. Two opposite speeches by others (சாவ, வாழ்க) close the verse, so a life is judged by what is said of it.

items.claim: remembering the house one was born into is part of living well
holding firmly to oneself is part of living well
knowing how one is regarded by others is part of living well
not living so that others wish one dead is part of living well
living so that the worthy wish one long years is good

68.reading: The verse names four practices (drawing out and cutting short, long bathing in the waters of a ghat, and staying in by day) that do not remove the blemish, and says that one who leaves these four and restrains the five senses, wanting nothing, is released.
68.nuance: The verse has two counts, நான்கு and ஐந்து: four rejected practices and the restraint of the five senses that it approves; they are given as five items, the last of a different kind. What is drawn out and cut short (food, hair, the body) is not said, and வேகும்பம் on line 4 is unclear.

items.claim: drawing out (a practice) does not remove the blemish
cutting short (a practice) does not remove the blemish
long bathing in the ghat's waters does not remove the blemish
staying in by day does not remove the blemish
restraining the five senses, wanting nothing, brings release

69.reading: The verse names five who share in a killing (the one who killed, the one who agreed to it, the one who took the killed thing without hesitation when it was fat, the one who cooked it and the one who ate it when served) and says the sin should be reckoned as bound on all five.
69.nuance: The chain runs from the act to the meal, and the eater, last, is the one least likely to think himself guilty; the verse closes the gap the eater relies on.

items.claim: the one who killed bears the sin
the one who agreed to the killing bears the sin
the one who took the killed creature bears the sin
the one who cooked it bears the sin
the one who ate it when served bears the sin

norm.note: the Jain rule against flesh-eating of the period, stated as a share in the sin of killing

70.reading: The verse names five kinds of people (those lying in prison, those who fast for the ... (perhaps the dead), those who have lain many days in ..., those who eat only every other day, and those who eat nothing from the crescent to the full moon) and says that those who gave to them will live as kings in all fullness.
70.nuance: Four of the five are fasters by vow; the prisoner, first, goes hungry by force, so the list joins chosen and imposed hunger. செந்தார்க்கு and உறைக்கிடந்தார் are uncertain (செந்தார் may stand for செத்தார், the dead).

items.claim: giving to those lying in prison brings kingship
giving to those who fast for (perhaps) the dead brings kingship
giving to those who have lain confined many days brings kingship
giving to those who eat on alternate days brings kingship
giving to those who fast from the crescent to the full moon brings kingship

71.reading: The verse lists five acts that, it says, the authors of the old books declared great virtue: delivering a child, caring for a pregnant woman, taking up an infant, sheltering in one's house an unmarried girl who has conceived, and sheltering a man who is ruined.
71.nuance: The verse appeals to authority (முதுநூலார்) rather than to a fruit. The unmarried pregnant girl is counted among those to be taken in, not cast out; the verse names her condition plainly.

items.claim: delivering a child is great virtue
caring for a pregnant woman is great virtue
taking up an infant is great virtue
sheltering an unmarried girl who has conceived is great virtue
sheltering a ruined man in one's house is great virtue

norm.note: a period view of the unmarried girl who has conceived, whom the verse counts it great virtue to shelter

72.reading: The verse says that a single mouthful given, without asking who they are, to those who have lost their strength, the old, those who sit facing north to die, those wasted by disease, and those ruined by losing their land, makes the giver a king.
72.nuance: இன்னவராம் என்னாராய், 'not asking who they are', makes the gift blind to the recipient's worth, in a book that elsewhere rewards gifts to ascetics. வடக்கிருந்தார், those who sit facing north to die, stand here among the needy rather than the heroic.

items.claim: a mouthful given to those who have lost their strength makes the giver a king
a mouthful given to the old makes the giver a king
a mouthful given to those who sit facing north to die makes the giver a king
a mouthful given to those wasted by disease makes the giver a king
a mouthful given to those ruined by the loss of their land makes the giver a king

73.reading: The verse lists acts of care around birth (guarding the pregnant woman from distress, not neglecting her when the embryo is harmed, help at the delivery, taking up the infant without shrinking from it, medicine for the child, and not frightening it) and says that, examined, the greatness of virtue lies in these.
73.nuance: The verse has no count word. It is divided here into six on the six negated or verbal nouns, but விலங்காமைக் கோடல் may join குழவி, and இலங்காமை after கருப்பஞ் சிதைந்தால் is unclear, so five is as defensible.

items.claim: guarding the pregnant woman from distress is great virtue
not neglecting her when the embryo is harmed is great virtue
help at the delivery is great virtue
taking up the newborn without shrinking from it is great virtue
medicine for the infant is great virtue
not frightening the infant is great virtue

74.reading: The verse sets out the pains of bringing a life into being (failing to conceive, the suffering of pregnancy, being unable to nurse after the birth, the hardship of rearing once begun, and the incapacity that follows) and says that those who know these well find, on sifting, that not eating and not killing are good.
74.nuance: The five pains are given as items; the predicate the verse draws from them is உண்ணாமை and கொல்லாமை. உண்ணாமை is read as not eating flesh, beside not killing, but it may mean fasting. ஏலாமை and சால்பவை வல்லாமை are uncertain.

items.claim: failing to conceive is one of the pains the wise weigh
the suffering of pregnancy is one of the pains the wise weigh
being unable (to nurse) after the birth is one of the pains the wise weigh
the hardship of rearing once undertaken is one of the pains the wise weigh
the incapacity that follows is one of the pains the wise weigh

norm.note: the Jain abstention from eating flesh and killing of the period, argued from the pains of bearing life

75.reading: The verse says that those who in former days cured the gathered diseases of five kinds of sufferer (சிக்கர், the blind or dull, those whose mouths are eaten as by termites, the afflicted, and those with piles) now live free of any disease.
75.nuance: முன்னாளில் and இந்நாள் are read as an earlier birth and this one: present health is the fruit of past healing. The disease words (சிக்கர், சிதடர், துக்கர், துருநாமர்) are rare and their senses are uncertain.

items.claim: curing the சிக்கர் earns a life without disease
curing the blind or dull earns a life without disease
curing those whose mouths are eaten as by termites earns a life without disease
curing the afflicted earns a life without disease
curing those with piles earns a life without disease

76.reading: The verse names five duties: not taking sides, taking on another's suffering, not being swayed, giving food to the hungry even if they are the low who are not worthy ascetics, and holding back excessive anger.
76.nuance: The fourth item ranks recipients (தவமல்லாத் தக்கார், இழியினர்) and then sets the ranking aside: the hungry are fed even if low. இழியினர் here ranks people; it may be birth-rank or low conduct. தக்கம் படாமை and பாடேற்றல் are uncertain.

items.claim: not taking sides is a duty
taking on suffering for another is a duty
not being swayed is a duty
giving food to the hungry, even the low, is a duty
holding back excessive anger is a duty

norm.note: a ranking of recipients by worth and lowness (இழியினர்) of the period, which the verse sets aside for the hungry

77.reading: The verse says that those who gave to the wounded, to those with no one to care for them, to those whose life is ebbing, to those who have lost their eyes and to those without both legs, people sunk and broken, will live gladly to the end.
77.nuance: Line 3 (ஆழ்ந்து நெகிழ்ந்தவர்க்கு) sums the five as those sunk and broken; it is read as a summary, not a sixth item.

items.claim: giving to the wounded brings a glad life to the end
giving to those with no one to care for them brings a glad life to the end
giving to those whose life is ebbing brings a glad life to the end
giving to those who have lost their eyes brings a glad life to the end
giving to those without both legs brings a glad life to the end

78.reading: The verse names five who live beyond eighty: one who shares his food in a time of famine, one who does not hoard, one who goes fearlessly into a breaking army and strikes, one who gives before he eats and holds nothing back, and one who makes offerings for children.
78.nuance: The list joins the householder's sharing with the soldier's courage under one reward, long life. காவாதான் may belong with the next clause (one who, not guarding himself, enters the army), and குழவி பலிகொடுப்பான் may be one who feeds children or one who offers for them.

items.claim: one who shares his food in famine lives beyond eighty
one who does not hoard lives beyond eighty
one who goes fearlessly into a breaking army and strikes lives beyond eighty
one who gives before he eats lives beyond eighty
one who makes offerings for children lives beyond eighty

79.reading: The verse lists what the wise (implied) shun: they do not keep a woman without bounds, do not climb an anthill, do not befriend the worthless or a warring king, do not go where a fierce elephant like a hill is let loose, and do not travel the road where a cruel tiger prowls.
79.nuance: The list sets people (a woman without bounds, the worthless, the warring king) among natural dangers (anthill, elephant, tiger), so the human ones are read as hazards of the same kind. வையார் may mean 'do not keep' or 'do not revile', and மன்னைப்புற்று is unclear. The verse has no count word; six are given.

items.claim: a woman without bounds is shunned
climbing an anthill is shunned
friendship with the worthless is shunned
friendship with a warring king is shunned
the place where a fierce elephant is let loose is shunned
the road where a cruel tiger prowls is shunned

norm.note: a period view that sets the woman 'without bounds' among dangers to be shunned

80.reading: The verse says the way of the worthy does not perish while the unworthy sink on a fallen way; blame and fame come from one's company, but understanding comes from one's own mind.
80.nuance: The last two lines divide what company governs (reputation) from what it does not (மதி, understanding). The count of five is a reading of a verse without a count word.

items.claim: the way of the worthy does not perish
the unworthy sink on a fallen way
blame comes from one's company
fame comes from one's company
understanding comes from one's own mind

links.note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to living in a hut with a snake; the verse names five such housemates and calls them a disease.
links.teaches: Read together, the couplet's unnamed discordant housemates become a roster of the house (kin, wife, servant, son, neighbour), so the inner enemy is located in the very people one cannot leave.
links.list_adds: It names five separate relations of the house and makes them one kind, a disease within, where the couplet leaves 'those not in accord' unnamed.

links.note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a village tank full of water; the verse makes the gift of water itself the first of five charities.
links.teaches: The Kural's tank is a figure for wealth all may draw on; the verse makes it literal and the lowest step of a scale that ends in founding temples and halls.
links.list_adds: It ranks the charities from a drink of water to founded buildings and puts a condition on charity at home, which the couplet's single image lacks.

links.note: Both verses list works for others' use of water, land and shelter; 62 promises great enjoyment, 65 heaven.
links.teaches: Together they mark a scale of public works and fruits: water, shade and halls bring enjoyment, while tanks, roads and wells bring heaven itself.

links.note: Naladiyar 99 says never call a gift too little, for like the ascetic's bowl it fills slowly; the verse lists the pittances (a handful, begged salt, a rag) given without calling them small.
links.teaches: The quatrain argues from the receiver's slowly filled bowl and the verse from the poor giver's actual pittances, so the same rule on small gifts is seen from both ends of the gift.
links.list_adds: It names five concrete pittances, salt the giver himself begged and a torn rag among them, so the rule is tested on gifts a beggar could make.

links.note: 63 says small gifts not called small bear great fruit; 64 names the melting of the giver's heart as what makes a small gift grow like a hill.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the first verse sets the gift's size aside and the second names what replaces it as the measure, the melting of the giver's heart.

links.note: Naladiyar 38 says a small gift grows vast when it reaches worthy hands; the verse says it grows like a hill when the giver's heart melts.
links.teaches: Both say a small gift grows huge but place the cause differently: the Naladiyar in the worth of the receiver, Sirupanchamoolam in the melted heart of the giver.
links.list_adds: It gives five images of melting as the measure of the giver's heart, a condition on the giver that the quatrain does not state.

links.note: Purananuru 18 urges the Pandya Nedunchezhiyan to build up tanks where the land dips, for those who bind water win wealth hereafter, sole rule and fame; the verse makes tank-digging one of five works that take any doer to heaven.
links.teaches: The duty the Sangam poet urged on one king becomes in the ethics work a merit open to any man of means, and the promised reward narrows from rule and fame to heaven.

links.note: Thirikadugam 16 counts one who digs a well of drinking water without stint among three who gain a body that does not die; the verse counts a shared well among five works leading to heaven.
links.teaches: The two counted works reward the same well differently, one with a deathless name in this world and the other with heaven, so the group divides on where the fruit of public works falls.

links.note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; the verse lists five ascetic forms and says that in the Kali age renunciation is false and the household alone true.
links.teaches: The couplet discounts the ascetic's marks but keeps renunciation, while the verse, for its own age, discounts renunciation itself, so one critique of outward form reaches opposite ends.
links.list_adds: It names five ascetic forms where the couplet names two, and ties its judgement to an age (கலி), which the couplet does not.

links.note: Kural 49 says that what is called virtue is household life; the verse ends that in the Kali age household life alone is true.
links.teaches: Both favour the household, but the Kural grounds it in what virtue is and the Jain verse in the corruption of the age, so one preference has a timeless and an historical ground.
links.list_adds: It reaches the household's primacy by eliminating a list of ascetic forms, a route the couplet does not take.

links.note: 66 rejects the outward marks of ascetics; 68 rejects four austerities and keeps only restraint of the five senses.
links.teaches: Together the two verses strip ascetic display in two moves, first the marks on the body and then its austerities, leaving only restraint of the senses.

links.note: Kural 240 says those who live without blame are the ones who live; the verse names the means of a life the worthy bless, beginning with remembering one's birth-house.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the verdict of blame and fame on a life and the verse the means of earning the good verdict, so memory of lineage becomes a guard on reputation.
links.list_adds: It sets lineage, self-hold and awareness of others' regard as causes of the good name the couplet only judges, ending on two opposed speeches of others.

links.note: Kural 343 says the field of the five must be crushed and all desire let go; the verse sets restraint of the five and wanting nothing against four rejected practices.
links.teaches: The verse supplies what the couplet leaves out, the practices that do not count, so restraint of the senses is defined against bathing and bodily austerity rather than only stated.
links.list_adds: It sets the couplet's restraint of the five against four rejected practices, a contrast the couplet lacks.

links.note: Kural 256 says that if none killed to eat, none would sell flesh; the verse divides the sin among killer, consenter, taker, cook and eater.
links.teaches: The couplet ties the eater to the seller by demand; the verse spreads the sin along the whole chain, so even one who only consented or only cooked is guilty.
links.list_adds: It names five links of the chain and makes them one guilt, where the couplet names only the eater and the seller.

links.note: Kural 225 ranks the strength of enduring hunger behind the strength of removing it; the verse names kinds of fasters and promises kingship to those who feed them.
links.teaches: The couplet ranks feeder over faster, while the verse honours both, making the faster the fit receiver and the feeder the one rewarded, so the ranking becomes a partnership.
links.list_adds: It names kinds of fasting (alternate days, crescent to full moon) and sets the prisoner among them, and attaches kingship as the reward, which the couplet does not.

links.note: 71 counts delivering a child, caring for the pregnant and taking up an infant as great virtue; 73 sets out the care of pregnancy, birth and infancy step by step.
links.teaches: Together the two verses make care of mother and newborn a sequence of virtues, from sheltering the pregnant to medicine for the child, which the Kural does not treat.

links.note: Purananuru 219 addresses a warrior wasting his body as he sits to die, with many sitting with him; the verse counts those who sit facing north among the needy to be fed.
links.teaches: The act the Puram honours as heroic resolve the Jain ethics verse counts as a state of need beside age and disease, so the dying hero becomes a receiver of care.

links.note: 69 argues against flesh from the shared sin of the chain of killing; 74 argues for not eating and not killing from the pains of bearing and rearing a life.
links.teaches: The book gives two grounds for one abstention: the guilt that runs from killer to eater, and the cost of bringing any life into being.

links.note: Naladiyar 123 says the old deed of breaking crabs' legs returns as a disease that rots the fingers; the verse says those who once cured disease now live free of it.
links.teaches: Read together, disease and health are both the return of old deeds, cruelty coming back as rotting fingers and healing as a body without illness, so the law runs both ways.
links.list_adds: It names five kinds of sufferer cured and makes healing a merit whose fruit is health, where the quatrain gives only the punishment.

links.note: 70 promises kingship to those who feed fasting ascetics; 76 makes feeding the hungry a duty even to the low who are not ascetics.
links.teaches: The book first rewards gifts to ascetics who fast, then widens the duty past them, so the receiver's worth governs the reward but not the obligation to feed.

links.note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is true giving; the verse makes feeding the hungry a duty even when they are low and not ascetics.
links.teaches: The couplet defines giving by the receiver's need; the verse tests that against rank and lets need prevail over lowness and lack of austerity.
links.list_adds: It sets feeding the hungry among duties of impartiality and restraint of anger, and names the low receiver the couplet does not.

links.note: 72 promises kingship for one mouthful given to the weak, the old and the dying; 77 promises a glad life to the end for gifts to the wounded, blind and lame.
links.teaches: The two lists of the helpless overlap but name different rewards, showing the book attaches a distinct fruit to each list rather than one fixed reward for giving.

links.note: Kural 227 says hunger does not touch one used to sharing his food; the verse says one who shares his food in a famine lives beyond eighty.
links.teaches: The couplet promises the sharer freedom from hunger; the verse puts the sharing in a famine, when it costs most, and promises long life instead.
links.list_adds: It ranks famine-sharing with fearless fighting and giving before eating as one road to long life, joining the householder's and the soldier's merits.

links.note: Kural 691 tells those who join warring kings to be like men warming at a fire, neither far nor near; the verse sets the warring king among things the wise do not befriend, beside the elephant and the tiger.
links.teaches: The couplet teaches the courtier how to stand near the dangerous king; the verse, for one not bound to serve, says not to go near, so one danger yields a rule of distance and a rule of avoidance.
links.list_adds: It ranks the warring king with a loosed elephant and a prowling tiger, so the king is one more natural danger, not a master to be served.

links.note: Thirikadugam 19 counts one who grips the tusk of a killing elephant among three who hang by a thread; the verse shuns the place where a fierce elephant is let loose.
links.teaches: Both counted works use the killing elephant as the type of avoidable danger and set human follies beside it, so folly with people is measured against folly with beasts.

links.note: Kural 454 says understanding seems to be in the mind but lies in one's company; the verse says blame and fame come from company but understanding from the mind.
links.teaches: On the plain reading the two divide the same pair the opposite way: the Kural puts understanding in company, while Sirupanchamoolam keeps it in the mind and gives company only reputation.
links.list_adds: It splits the effect of company by kind, reputation (பழியும் புகழும்) against understanding (மதி), a division the couplet does not make.

links.note: Naladiyar 245 says people are not as their kind but as their minds; the verse keeps understanding in the mind while granting company power over blame and fame.
links.teaches: With the Naladiyar the verse forms a Jain answer to the Kural's chapter on company: mind, not kind, decides what a person is, though the verse concedes that company decides their name.
links.list_adds: It concedes to company what the quatrain does not, blame and fame, while agreeing that the mind decides understanding.

links.note: Naladiyar 180 says people spotless in mind are scorned for their company, as sandal burns with the scrub; the verse says blame and fame come from company.
links.teaches: The quatrain shows the cost the verse only states: a spotless mind does not save one from the blame of one's company.
links.list_adds: It states the rule in two halves, company for name and mind for understanding, where the quatrain gives only the half on reputation.

source_issues: 61 line 1: அடங்காய் and பெண்வியக்க are hard to construe; the reading of the first three items is uncertain.
63 line 3: சிதவலிப்(பு) is unclear; read as சிதவல் (a rag).
66 line 2: ஓர்த்(து) பால்மறைத்(து) உண்பான்மேய் is obscure and may be corrupt.
70 line 1: செந்தார்க்கு may be a misreading of செத்தார்க்கு.
76: the site lacks this verse (text flag site_diff), so it rests on one source.
77 line 2: கண்கண்பட்(டு) looks like a doubled syllable.
78 line 4: வாண் is probably a misprint for வார்.
